summary: Mission Ares-I is a 2D pixel art video game created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Challenge 13: Space Mission Design Game). Players command a crew of four astronauts on a crewed mission to Jezero Crater on Mars, searching for ancient water and signs of past life. Before liftoff, you must design the spacecraft: budget, mass, power, data, communications and time all compete with one another, and improving one almost always means sacrificing another. Then come the launch, a radiation storm, the landing and the rover exploration, with difficult decisions that affect the crew, the science and the resources. Nothing comes free: the final score reflects mission success, the science gathered, efficiency and the quality of your decisions. Each run lasts about 10 minutes and ends differently depending on the choices you make, including failure, which the game treats as a lesson rather than a punishment. Inspired by NASA’s Design and Develop Science Missions guide and by Perseverance’s exploration of Jezero, the game brings real mission engineering closer to students. Its impact is educational: it teaches players to weigh trade-offs, work as a team and persevere, and shows that failing is part of engineering and that space exploration belongs to everyone.
details:
What it does and how it works

Misión Ares-I: Design, Launch and Survive is a 2D pixel-art game in the style of Terraria, where the player designs and flies a crewed mission to Jezero Crater on Mars in search of ancient water.

The game begins with a briefing where you meet the crew — Dan, Ana, Leo and Maya — each with a role: Ana leads science, Leo runs engineering and power, and Maya handles communications and data. There you choose a difficulty (Rookie with $700M, Engineer with $500M, or Director with $400M) and a science objective: search for ancient water, map the crater, or fly a low-cost mission. Next, you design the spacecraft at four workshop stations (rocket, power, instruments, and communications/orbit), balancing six resources that update in real time: mass, power, budget, data, communications and time.

Then comes the flight. The launch lasts 12 seconds and requires keeping thrust in the green zone (60–85%). It is followed by a transit through a debris belt and a solar storm with three options, and then a 15-second powered descent with retrorockets (EDL), where you must brake to touch down at 2.5 m/s or less. The final phase is the rover exploration of Jezero, lasting 60 seconds: you drive, scan with the Space key, and drill up to 5 samples, none of them handed out for free. A decision at the ravine and a final engineering report — with a radar chart and a score breakdown — close out the mission.

The total score is 1,000 points, split across four categories: mission success (400), scientific value (300), resource efficiency (150) and decision quality (150). If the player abandons a stage, they earn 0 points for that part, so the result reflects only what was actually played.

Benefits

The game lets anyone try their hand at designing a space mission, with no engineering background required. It encourages systems thinking, because every decision has a cost, and teamwork, because the crew's skills matter in every phase. Each run lasts about 10 minutes and is highly replayable: different designs and decisions lead to different endings, including failure, which the game presents as part of engineering rather than a punishment.

Expected impact

We want players, especially students like us, to understand that space missions are built on trade-offs, not unlimited resources, and that science is a team effort. By playing with real constraints (budget, mass and power) and real science (Jezero Crater and Perseverance's search for signs of past life), players face the same questions NASA engineers ask. The game is also free, runs in the browser and needs no installation, so any classroom can use it.

Tools, languages and software

We built it in plain JavaScript (Vanilla JS) with HTML5 Canvas 2D, with no game engine. The pixel-art sprites (16×16 maps) are drawn through code, so the game runs without any image files. We used NASA's Design and Develop Science Missions guide as the basis for structuring the mission segments (launch, space, ground and user), and drew on data about Jezero and Perseverance as scientific context. We also used AI tools to review code, plan, and draft text, and to generate reference images and the team photo. The sprites, however, are generated by code and are not AI images.

Creativity

Our central idea was to turn a real engineering process into a game: the workshop is a set of trade-offs, the flight is a series of skill-based minigames, and the score is a report card that only rewards what you truly played. The Terraria-style pixel art makes a technical subject feel friendly, and the crew — four astronauts with different roles and a scene of human conflict — turns the mission into a story rather than a spreadsheet.

Factors the team considered

We treated the six resources of the challenge (mass, power, budget, data, communications and time) as a single system, so that no decision could break the game. We checked the science: only Perseverance is at Jezero (Curiosity is at Gale), and the Martian equivalent of geostationary orbit is areostationary. We deliberately kept the scope small, with one mission, three decisions and about 10 minutes of play, so that a student team could finish a polished prototype in a weekend. And we made failure fair: the only path that fails is the greedy one, and every run teaches something for the next
